title: Cheese-Making: A return to Hen Corner
text:
Cheese-Making: A return to Hen Corner
An Urban Small Holding near Twickenham Rugby Stadium; A soft Blue cheese, a fresh Garlic & Herb cheese & a squeaky Halloumi; Sara Ward’s recipe for easy peasy gluten free seeded cheese crackers
Introduction:
I adore cheese. Cheese with good bread is my go to solo supper.
I have previously written about cheese making with Silke Cropp at Broughgammon Farm on the Causeway Coast in summer 2024.
I wrote about cheese again in 2025 when I visited Fromagerie les Frères Bernard at La Ferme du Vert, near our French home in Wissant.
So you might say Cheese is one of my passions.
My all time favourite is Goats Cheese.
All the French chèvres and Irish Saint Tola from Inagh in the Burren, county Clare, where I first met the charming Meg and Derek Gordon on their magical goat farm in the 1990s.
Photo: Saint Tola
Not to forget Corleggy made by that pioneer cheese maker from county Cavan, Silke Cropp, whom I initially met at a farmers market in Westport in the mid 1980s.
Photo: Corleggy Cheeses
You can read more about goats, goat husbandry at Buttercups Sanctuary, regenerative farming at Broughgammon Farm and how I got on cooking Andi Oliver’s Curry Goat using cabrito (kid) meat here.
In second place, I would always choose a blue cheese. French Roquefort and two Irish cheeses come to mind: Cashel Blue from county Tipperary and Mike’s Fancy Cheese Young Buck from Newtownards in County Down.
Photo: Young Buck, Mike’s Fancy Cheese
Having shared my passion for cheese with you, I should point out that growing up in Ireland in the 1970s and 80s, cheese was limited to Cheddar. Welsh rarebit, Macaroni Cheese or a Cheese omelette. Done well - a fine supper fit for a King. Or a Jacob’s cream cracker, butter, cheddar and a slick of Branston pickle when you arrive home ravenous after school. What’s not to love?
But I do remember that when I visited our
Photo: Nana, Granddad and my godfather Uncle Roger as a child (cute)
grandparents, Nora and Tom Costello, on their dairy farm in Ballyglass West, a summer supper could contain lettuce, tomatoes, cucumber, scallions and what, as we children thought then, the rather exotic processed Irish cheese Calvita. Very yummy and nostalgic it was too.
Check out this retro 1970s Calvita Cheese advert.
The Origins of Hen Corner:
I first visited Hen Corner in February 2017.
I had recently left my 28 year teaching career behind me and started a new pathway into veterinary nursing. The work was physically demanding and the apprenticeship income was based on the minimum wage (£7.50 per hour at the time). Yet that didn’t stop me loving my new role.
Looking back now, I recognise that I was searching for a more meaningful, creative life. Working with animals was one important part of my journey. Yet I realised that writing, art and cheese making were equally important passions that I wished to explore and experience.
This is what brought me to Hen Corner in spring 2017, where Sara Ward taught me how to make Mozzarella, Feta and a mould ripened semi soft Camembert cheese.
Sara Ward herself was a former city banker. Always generous in sharing her own journey and the origins of Hen Corner, her story starts when she was weaning her young children. Sara kept asking herself “Where does our food come from?” As a parent, she wanted to feed their children organic food and reduce food waste. Sara and her husband were committed to consuming a smaller quantity of higher quality food.
So Sara began growing fruit and vegetables; keeping chickens; beekeeping and now has an allotment, in addition to their generous corner site Victorian garden in west London.
Here at Hen Corner, Sara makes jams, marmalades and chutneys. She pickles, salts and ferments vegetables and fruits. In addition to baking and selling sourdough breads and creating delicious cheeses.
Photos: author, From Left to Right in anticlockwise direction: Sara’s home made Quince jam, Goats cheese, Mimolette, Camembert, Stilton, farmhouse Cheddar and Emmental, that we gorged on at lunch with crusty bread.
In 2010, Sara began offering courses in making bread, cheeses and preserves at Hen Corner. She also visits schools, helping children to understand where different foods actually come from.
Sara’s urban small holding has been a runaway success, now producing approximately £5000 worth of food per year.
She has presented at the Gardeners’ World show, the Ideal Homes show and Country Living magazine fair.
In March this year, Sara appeared on Jimmy and Shivi’s Farmhouse Breakfast programme on ITV.
Video: YouTube
Sara wrote a series of monthly articles for the BBC Gardeners’ World magazine in 2025 and previously wrote a monthly column in Country Living magazine.
Country Living magazine July 2021
This is in addition to her own Hen Corner blog.
Sara and Hen Corner featured in this month’s July 2026 edition of Good Housekeeping Magazine:
July 2026 UK Good Housekeeping page 137
Sara is to be congratulated on writing and having her first book Living the Good Life in the City published in July 2023. Of course I had to buy a copy when I visited Hen Corner earlier this year.
Note to self: I really, really need to stop buying more books, until after we have moved into and unpacked in our new home on the island of Ireland (should be late September). Yet Elizabeth Strout’s latest novel The Things We Never Say keeps calling to me. I have been strong and resisted - so far. However, Lucy Hearne Keane’s monthly book review has just appeared in my inbox yesterday and she has given Strout’s latest novel an excellent review. My resolve is starting to waver.
But I digress. Back to cheese.
A very short alternative History of Cheese Making:
Humans have been making cheese for thousands of years.
Sara Ward likes to tell an alternative story about how humans may have accidentally discovered how to make cheese. She reminds us of the David and Goliath story in the Old Testament (Samuel 17). David is a shepherd boy, the youngest son of an Ephrathite named Jesse, who was from Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse has eight sons.
There is an ongoing war between the Israelites led by Saul and the Philistines, who have a nine foot giant called Goliath fighting for them.
David’s three older brothers, Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, are fighting for the Israelites but David, being the youngest, must stay at home to mind the sheep.
David’s elderly father Jesse instructs David to take ten loaves of bread and ten cheeses to his three eldest brothers and the Israelite army.
Painting: The Story of David and Goliath, Francesco Pesellino, c 1445 -1455, Wikipedia Commons
Now Sara Ward wonders whether it was likely that David took some milk with him for the journey for nourishment and to quench his thirst? At that time, liquids would have been carried in a natural bag made out of a washed and rinsed animal stomach, tied at both ends. And is it just possible that on David’s journey with the combination of the heat, the constant jostling movement of the milk inside the stomach bag and perhaps some remnant animal rennet inside the stomach that the milk might have coagulated and been turned into curds and whey?
It’s a nice story, isn’t it?
Now back to the facts:
In 2018, the BBC reported that a previously whitish substance found by archaeologists inside a broken jar in an ancient Egyptian tomb has been identified as 3200 year old cheese:
Ancient 3200 year old Cheese in Egyptian Tomb
Cheese has been depicted in artwork from at least the time of the Egyptians:
Grazing goats in a scene from the tomb of Ipuy (TT217). The goatherd carries a sack which could be a churning bag. A woman offers small white balls, possibly cheese, for sale in the marketplace. Image: facsimile painting by Norman de Garis Davies from Two Ramesside Tombs (1927) pl.XXXIV. Source:Hilary Wilson, the-past.com
Before the invention of refrigeration, humans used natural methods to preserve food beyond the time of harvest, foraging or slaughter. These methods included:
Drying (eg herbs, tomatoes, mushrooms, fruits)
Salting (eg fish, pork, olives, capers, lemons)
Pickling (eg fruit, vegetables, fish)
Fermenting (eg wine, beer, bread, cheese, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi)
I have written previously about making bread, wine and beer. All three processes involve fermentation.
So what actually is fermentation?
A quick reminder of some school science.
In aerobic respiration, glucose is converted into energy, water and carbon dioxide.
Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
Fermentation is anaerobic respiration - where there is no oxygen present.
Think about if you have ever exercised or ran so fast that you were unable to breathe in sufficient oxygen rich air? In this case, oxygen does not reach all the cells in your body to produce the required energy. When this happens, anaerobic respiration kicks in. One byproduct of anaerobic respiration is lactic acid, which can generate an uncomfortable ache in your muscles.
If oxygen is not available to animal cells then pyruvate is converted into lactate (sometimes referred to as lactic acid).
Glucose → Lactate + Energy
In plant and yeast cells, pyruvate is converted into carbon dioxide and a type of alcohol called ethanol.
Glucose → Carbon dioxide + Ethanol + Energy
So making bread, wine, beer and cheese all involve fermentation.
Cheese making, because it involves animal cells (ie milk), produces lactic acid - which gives cheese that lovely tanginess.
Before we commenced making our three cheeses for the day, Sara emphasised that all cheeses require the same three things - milk (from mammals), salt and heat.
The salt helps regulate the flavour of the cheese, but in addition, the salt controls the fermentation process, kills unwanted bacteria and helps to remove moisture from the cheese.
The variation between cheeses is due to three factors - temperature, time and technique.
Sara clarified the differences between raw milk, pasteurised milk, whole milk, unhomogenised milk and organic milk.
Unpasteurised (Raw) Milk:
In the past, all cheeses would have been made from raw milk - milk that has not been pasteurised. In France, this milk is described as lait cru. I can still remember the rich, creamy taste of the warm milk fresh from the zinc pail my grandfather Tom used to milk his cows by hand. Some cheese lovers, myself included, would argue that a properly high quality cheese made from raw, unpasteurised milk has a far superior taste to one made with pasteurised milk.
Pasteurised Milk:
Pasteurisation was invented by Louis Pasteur, a French scientist, in 1863, whilst working on the problem of wine contaminated by microbes.
Pasteurisation involves heating the milk to a minimum of 72 degrees Celsius for a minimum of 15 seconds, before rapidly cooling the liquid to 4 to 5 degrees Celsius.
Today, pasteurisation is widely used to kill any harmful bacteria and to extend milk’s shelf life.
Organic Milk:
Organic milk comes from cows that have a high welfare life, spending most of their time outside eating grass, all feed is organic and the cows do not receive routine antibiotics.
Whole Milk:
The cream in milk has a higher fat content, is less dense and therefore rises to the top of a bottle of milk. Do you remember the bottles of gold top milk left by the milkman on your front door step?
Garden birds loved to break the gold foil and enjoy an early morning treat. Sadly now, a dying occurrence with the demise of the milkman and his van.
For lower fat milk such as semi - skimmed or skimmed, this cream is partially or fully skimmed off.
Unhomogenised Milk:
Homogenisation is the process of blitzing up whole milk so that the size of the fat globules is reduced, thus creating a more even distribution of the fat throughout the milk. This process stops the cream rising to the top of a bottle of whole milk.
Sara Ward believes that unhomogenised whole milk makes a better cheese.
Why do you need to add Starter, Rennet and particular Bacteria to the warmed Milk?
The mesophilic starter is necessary because of the pasteurisation process - which destroys both good and bad bacteria. The starter culture encourages the good bacteria in the milk to flourish and aids curd formation. Once opened, store your mesophilic starter in the freezer.
Rennet is traditionally found in the stomach lining of a sheep. Today you can purchase vegetarian rennet, which once opened can last in the fridge for a few years.
The Penicillium Roqueforti culture is used to develop the blue veins in cheese. The bacteria need warmth, air and humidity to grow. This bacterium culture can be stored in the freezer for 2 years.
Sara Ward’s Fresh Garlic and Herb Roule Cheese:
This is an easy crowd pleaser. Soft and creamy, garlicky and cool - with a fresh herb spiral throughout.
Ingredients:
4 pints (2 litres) Organic Whole Milk (unhomogenised if possible).
Mesophilic Starter (adds back good bacteria after pasteurisation, use quantities as stated on packet).
Rennet (we used liquid vegetarian) - use half the quantity stated on packet.
2 cloves of garlic, minced.
1 tsp salt
Fresh herbs - dependent on season. I like chives or basil. But you could use rocket, nasturtium leaves - whatever you fancy.
Method:
Dissolve the rennet (half quantity as on packet) in half a cup of cool boiled water.
Gently warm the milk to 30 degrees Celsius, add the mesophilic starter on the top surface of the milk, following instructions on the pack, stir gently, add diluted rennet in a zig-zag pattern across the top of the milk and gently stir using a large slotted spoon with holes, up and down. Cover and leave to slowly set for 5 hours or overnight.
Photo: author
Gently pour the curds into a colander lined with cheesecloth or a clean tea towel, collecting the whey in a bowl underneath. Tie the corners of the cloth and hang the bag for 5 hours or overnight.
Photo: author
Unwrap the curds, tip into a bowl and stir in the salt and minced garlic, combining well.
Photo: author
Spread the seasoned curds on the cheesecloth to form a rectangle, sprinkle with the chopped fresh herbs and roll up carefully forming a spiral. This was as challenging as it looks - quite fiddly actually.
Wrap the cheese in the cloth and allow to drain/dry on a piece of paper towel. We used Japanese sushi mats - which can be bought cheaply in most supermarkets.
This fresh Roule cheese can be eaten straight away or stored in the fridge.
Photo: author
In addition, I placed some of the curds in a heart shaped cheese mould; draining well before eventually turning upside down just like making a sandcastle and then sprinkling the soft cheese with charcoal ash provided by Sara. I was a little heavy handed sprinkling the charcoal ash.
Photo: author
Sara Ward’s Squeaky Halloumi:
This is the perfect grilled cheese, great for kebabs and barbecues. Once made, you can store it in brine in the fridge until you need it. But I don’t think it will last that long - it’s so moreish rolled in herbs or spices and fried in the pan.
Ingredients:
8 pints (4 litres) Organic Whole Milk (unhomogenised if possible).
Mesophilic Starter - use quantities as stated on packet.
Rennet (we used liquid vegetarian) - use quantities as stated on packet.
2 tbsp salt for sprinkling.
Brine for storage (1 litre water + 250g salt).
Method:
Dissolve the rennet (quantity as on the packet) in half a cup of cool boiled water.
Gently warm the milk to 30 degrees Celsius, add the mesophilic starter across the surface of the milk, stir gently, add diluted rennet and gently stir, up and down, for one minute.
Cover and leave to set for 45 minutes. The milk will have coagulated to a solid gel like form. Cut the curds into 1cm cubes using a long knife and cutting from different angles.
Slowly increase the temperature, by 2 degrees every 5 mins, until the curds reach 40 degrees Celsius, stirring gently. Maintain at 40 degrees Celsius for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Ladle the curds into a cheesecloth lined colander, reserving the whey.
Pack the curds into a cloth lined mould and press for 1 hour, remove from mould, redress, turn and return to mould - press for 30 minutes.
Heat the whey to 90 degrees Celsius. Remove cheese from the mould and cut into 10cm square blocks.
Place the cheese blocks in the hot whey to soak for 1 hour (when they rise to float, turn them over).
Remove the blocks of cheese from the whey, allow to cool for 20 minutes, sprinkle with salt and cool for 1 hour.
Photo: author
Store in brine until needed.
Serve grilled. At home, I rolled my sliced Halloumi in two different spices before grilling in a pan. My first chosen spice was smoked paprika and for variety, I rolled the other half of my sliced halloumi in za’atar. Other alternatives could include crushed black peppercorns, crushed coriander seeds, cumin seeds or whatever your tastebuds desire.
Sara Ward’s Soft Mould Ripened Blue Cheese:
Soft and creamy with a blue tang... this is definitely something to be proud of making.
Ingredients:
4 pints (2 litres) Organic Whole Milk (unhomogenised if possible)
Mesophilic Starter - use quantities as stated on packet
Penicillium Roqueforti - use quantities as stated on packet
Rennet (we used liquid vegetarian) - use the quantity as stated on packet
1 tbspn salt for sprinkling
Method:
Dissolve the rennet in half a cup of cool boiled water.
Gently warm the milk to 35 degrees Celsius, add the mesophilic starter, following instructions on the pack, stir gently, cover and leave to ripen for 1 hour.
Add Penicillium Roqueforti and stir through, add diluted rennet and gently stir, up and down. Cover and leave to set for 30 minutes.
Cut the curds into 2cm cubes using a long knife cutting from different angles, stir gently, cover and leave to rest for 1 hour.
Ladle the curds into a cloth lined colander, leave to drain for 20 minutes, sprinkle with 1 tsp salt.
Transfer to a cloth lined mould, place in a sealed plastic container in the fridge, draining the whey daily.
After one week, remove cheese from both cloth and the mould, sprinkle with salt and piece air holes with a long needle from all sides to allow the blue mould to grow. Store on a cheese mat in a sealed container in the fridge.
Photo: author, my blue cheese at 8 weeks
After 2 weeks the blue mould will have developed and it’s ready to eat.
I have to confess - I left my soft mould ripened blue cheese in my fridge for longer than two weeks, as I wished to develop a richer flavour. I checked my cheese every morning - draining any extracted liquid (that took 10 days for me) and regularly turning my cheese before placing it back in its tall plastic container and returning to the fridge. Keeping the cheese inside a tall plastic container helps maintain the humidity necessary for the cheese to develop. I left the lid of my plastic container a little loose, not completely sealed.
Checking the dates on my digital photos, I can see that I allowed my blue cheese to develop for nine weeks four days before I could no longer resist cracking into my first born blue cheese.
Photo: author
I was very pleased with the gooey melt in the mouth texture and the distinctive blue cheese flavour. However, I would have wished for a greater concentration of blue veins in my cheese.
Sara had warned us about this challenge. When I initially filled my cheese mould with the curds at Hen Corner, it really felt like King David said: “my cup runneth over” (Psalm 23: 5 - 6).
Painting: King David, Giovanni Francesco Barbieri (il Guercino), 1651, Wikimedia Commons
My cheese mould was filled to the brim with curds. Yet with the passing of time, the downward force of gravity and the extraction of any residual whey from the cheese, the cheese reduces in size considerably.
By the time I came to piercing my cheese in all directions with a kebab skewer sterilised in boiling water one week later, I was afraid that if I continued to repeatedly pierce the reduced size cheese that it would collapse and crumble.
I remembered Sara’s words. You need sufficient holes through the cheese so that the air can circulate and the Penicillium Roqueforti mould can grow. But I lost my nerve and stopped piercing additional holes in my delicate cheese. Hindsight is a great thing.
Still, my cheese was delicious and I was quite proud of my achievement.
Sara Ward’s gluten-free Seeded Cheese Crackers:
Sara’s crackers were the perfect accompaniment to my fabulous homemade cheese. And they were so easy to make!
Ingredients:
100g Mixed Seeds
40g Polenta
10g Oil
3g Salt
100g Boiling water
Method:
Preheat the oven to 180 degrees Celsius.
Mix your dry ingredients in a bowl, pour over the boiling water, leave to rest for 5 minutes and then stir well.
Roll the mixture very thin between two sheets of baking parchment, then remove the top sheet.
Carefully transfer the bottom sheet of parchment, with the mixture, to a baking sheet.
Cut into rectangles, easing the seeds apart if needed.
Bake for 18 - 20 minutes until the seeds start to toast.
Cool on a rack, gently separating biscuits.
Photo: author
What to do with Whey - a waste product of Cheese Making:
Farmers sometimes feed leftover whey to their pigs. The Italians use whey to make that sublime soft fresh cheese ricotta by reheating the whey. In dried form, powdered whey is sometimes used by athletes as a protein supplement. Personally, I use any left over whey to make Irish soda bread, as an alternative to soured milk, buttermilk or yoghurt. Whey also freezes very well.
Reflections:
Photo: Sara Ward, Hens Corner
This was a truly satisfying creative day; I learnt so much and I met some very interesting people.
Photo: author
The experience has motivated me to further develop my cheese making skills and explore the possibility of starting a very small scale farmers market stall selling tiny fresh soft goats cheese bouchons, rolled in herbs, garlic, shallot or cracked black pepper, like these:
Photo: La Fromagerie en Herbe, Wissant
I will be returning to visit Silke Cropp, champion Cavan cheese maker on her own farm outside Belturbet in mid October this autumn to follow this dream of mine further.
I just hope that we will have moved in and unpacked in our new home by then. Fingers and toes crossed. September and October are going to be very busy.
Next time, I will be writing about a charming small town Bergues in Hauts de France, where the film Bienvenue Chez les Ch’tis was filmed in 2008.
Image: IMDb
I do hope you can join me.
